extracted.intended_audience: aspiring short-story writers submitting to literary magazines (slush-pile submitters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and preparing short-story submissions to literary magazines, based on Ploughshares first-readers' accounts of what stands out and what gets rejected in the slush pile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and Voice (Primary)
rubrics_metrics.description: It's not the subject matter but the way it's written that stands out; almost always more taken with language than with plot. 'The sentence is the unit of judgment; voice precedes content.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentence-level craft is decisive: do something distinctive at the sentence level. Voice should feel authentic and lead the reader; language should be the primary claim on attention even before plot. Examples/notes: readers notice small sentence-level risks or distinct phrasings; lack of voice is a common reason to pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Impact / Provoking Feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should make the reader feel, not merely think. 'The stories I pass on don't make me think; they make me feel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer narratives that center on a character's sensory experience and evoke longing or emotional stakes from page one. Evaluation: does the story provoke feeling rather than solely intellectual interest?

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Pacing — 'Pacing That Disappears'
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story is paced well, the reader forgets they are turning the page; pacing should disappear into the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good pacing keeps momentum and attention; poor pacing (including endings that 'peter out') is a common rejection reason. Assess scene length, beats, and whether the reader loses awareness of reading because the flow is natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid Setting / Immediate Spatial Orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spatial orientation must be immediate; reading without a good sense of space and location is disorienting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few precise sensory details establish setting — avoid long paragraphs of description. Evaluate whether the story gives an immediate, stable sense of place and sensory world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to Characters / Early Care
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader needs to care what happens to the characters early on; curiosity about events without care for people fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the story generates emotional investment in characters quickly (by characterization, stakes, sensory detail). If readers don't care about the people, plot tension alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-Page Hold / Immediate Claim on Attention
rubrics_metrics.description: A story must claim attention from the first page and hold it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-page hold is critical in the slush pile: evaluate initiation (opening sentence/paragraph), how the opening establishes voice, stakes, or sensory detail, and whether curiosity or emotional pull is sustained beyond the opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of Approach (Not Mere Subject Novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be different — not in subject, but in approach; subject matter pitched as edgy but written conventionally reads as gimmick over craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the story takes a distinctive formal, tonal, or syntactic approach to its material rather than relying on trendy or provocative subject matter alone. Look for craft choices that make a familiar subject feel necessary and fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity — 'Does this story have to exist?'
rubrics_metrics.description: A standout story feels necessary: 'like the writer had to write this story, this way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the story's choices (voice, structure, perspective) justify its existence — not merely competence but a sense that this particular telling is required. Consider whether the piece contributes something essential or inevitable rather than interchangeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism / Care Signals in Submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Care signals matter: formatting, proofreading, and restraint in cover letters reflect attention and care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid careless formatting and typos; remove track-changes and marginal notes; keep cover letters brief and do not summarize the plot (an over-elaborate cover letter suggests the story can't speak for itself). These technical/administrative issues are read as negligence and can doom a submission regardless of craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Clichés and Stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Clichés and stereotypes that feel flat or predictable are grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate specificity and originality of characterization, dialogue, metaphor, and plot choices. Flag language or situations that feel shopworn, predictably reductive, or stereotypical rather than particular and fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of Authenticity / Inauthentic Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of authenticity or a false/inauthentic voice is a common reason for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether voice feels earned and believable for the material and characters. Inauthentic register, forced mannerisms, or voice that doesn't convincingly belong to the speaker/character will undermine the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gimmick Over Craft (Subject Pitched as Edgy but Conventionally Written)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter pitched as edgy but written conventionally reads as a gimmick and is rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between true innovation in approach and mere topical shock value. If the work relies on an 'edgy' premise but uses standard craft without risky or fresh choices, it will likely fail to stand out.
